items.text: Okay, let's get started. Can everyone at the back hear me? Good. So last week we finished linear regression, and I left you with a question: we wrote down a loss function, the mean squared error, but we never actually said how a computer finds the weights that make that loss small. Today is all about answering that. So, quick recap. We have a model with parameters, I'll call them theta, that takes an input x and produces a prediction y hat. The loss function L of theta measures how wrong those predictions are on the training set. For regression we used mean squared error, the average of the squared differences between y hat and y. Now here's the important shift in perspective. Stop thinking of the loss as a function of the data. The data is fixed. Think of it as a function of theta. Every setting of the weights gives you one number, the loss, and training is just the search for the theta where that number is smallest.

For linear regression with squared error you can actually solve this in closed form. You set the derivative to zero and you get the normal equations. But that involves inverting a matrix that is d by d, which costs roughly d cubed, and for a neural network there is no closed form at all. So we need something iterative. Something that starts with a guess and improves it a little at a time. And the picture I want you to have in your head is a landscape. Two weights on the horizontal axes, loss on the vertical axis, and we are standing somewhere on this surface trying to walk downhill. Sorry, is the landscape always shaped like a bowl, like the one you drew for linear regression?

Great question. For linear regression with squared error, yes, it's convex, it's a bowl, and there is exactly one minimum. For neural networks, no. The surface has many local minima, flat plateaus and saddle points. We'll come back to why that matters when we talk about stochastic gradient descent. But the local question is the same in both cases. If I'm standing at a point theta, and I can only see the ground right around my feet, which direction should I step to make the loss go down the fastest? And the answer to that question is the gradient. The gradient of L with respect to theta is just the vector of partial derivatives, one per parameter. Each entry tells you how much the loss changes if you nudge that one weight a tiny bit. And the key fact from multivariable calculus is that the gradient points in the direction of steepest ascent.

So if the gradient points uphill, we go the other way. That gives us the gradient descent update rule, and I'll write it on the board: theta new equals theta old minus eta times the gradient of L evaluated at theta old. That's it. That is the whole algorithm, repeated until it converges. Eta here is the learning rate, sometimes called the step size. It's a hyperparameter, meaning you choose it, the algorithm doesn't learn it. And honestly, choosing it well is probably the single most important practical decision you'll make when training a model. Let's look at what happens with different values. I've got a one dimensional example here, L of w equals w squared, so the gradient is two w and the minimum is at zero. Start at w equals one. With eta equal to point one, each step multiplies w by point eight, so we shrink smoothly toward zero.

Now try eta equal to point nine. Each step multiplies w by one minus one point eight, which is negative point eight. So w jumps to negative point eight, then positive point six four, and so on. It still converges, but it oscillates back and forth across the minimum. And with eta equal to one point one, the multiplier is negative one point two. The magnitude grows every step. We overshoot further and further and the loss blows up to infinity. If you ever see your loss turn into NaN in the first few iterations, a learning rate that is too large is the first suspect. Too small is also a problem, just a quieter one. With eta equal to point zero zero one you'll get there eventually, but it might take thousands of times more steps, and on a non convex surface you're more likely to stall on a plateau where the gradient is nearly zero.

In practice people pick the learning rate by trying a few values on a log scale, say one, point one, point zero one, point zero zero one, and watching the training loss for the first few hundred steps. Pick the largest one that still decreases the loss steadily. When do we stop? A few common rules. Stop when the gradient norm falls below some small tolerance, stop when the loss hasn't improved by more than some threshold for a while, or simply stop after a fixed number of iterations. Most deep learning code just uses a fixed budget of epochs. One more thing before we move on. Notice what each gradient descent step costs. To compute the gradient of the mean squared error, I have to sum a term over every training example. If I have a million examples, every single step touches all one million of them.

And that's the motivation for stochastic gradient descent. The loss is an average over examples, so the gradient is an average of per example gradients. Instead of computing the exact average, what if we pick one example at random and use its gradient as an estimate? That estimate is noisy, but it's unbiased. In expectation over which example you pick, it equals the true full batch gradient. So on average you're still heading downhill, you just take a much more wobbly path, and each step costs one example instead of a million. In practice, nobody uses a single example either. We use a mini-batch, typically somewhere between thirty two and five hundred twelve examples. You average the gradients over the batch. That reduces the variance of the estimate, and it maps really well onto GPUs, which are happy to process a whole batch in parallel.

Some vocabulary you need to get right for the quiz. One iteration, or one step, is one parameter update using one mini-batch. One epoch is one full pass over the training set. So with fifty thousand examples and a batch size of one hundred, one epoch is five hundred iterations. And you should shuffle the data at the start of every epoch. If your data is sorted, say all the cats and then all the dogs, the batches won't be representative and the gradient estimates will be biased in a systematic way, which is much worse than random noise. Now, earlier someone asked about local minima and saddle points. Here's the interesting part. The noise in SGD is actually helpful. A noisy step can kick you off a saddle point or out of a sharp, narrow minimum, where full batch gradient descent would just sit there with a gradient of almost zero.

The flip side is that with a constant learning rate, SGD never fully settles. It keeps bouncing around in a region near the minimum. That's why people decay the learning rate over training, start large to make fast progress, then shrink it so the iterates can settle down. Okay. So we now have an algorithm, mini-batch SGD, and everything depends on one ingredient: the gradient of the loss with respect to every weight. For linear regression I could work that out by hand. For a network with millions of weights, we need a systematic way. That's backpropagation. Backpropagation is not a new learning algorithm. I want to be really clear about that. It is just an efficient way of computing gradients, using the chain rule from calculus, organised so that we never compute the same thing twice.

Let's start with the chain rule. If y is a function of u, and u is a function of x, then d y by d x equals d y by d u times d u by d x. You multiply the local derivatives along the path. Every one of you has done this in calculus, we're just going to do it very systematically. To be systematic, we draw a computational graph. Each node is one simple operation, like a multiply, an add, or a sigmoid. Edges carry values from one operation to the next. The forward pass walks the graph from the inputs to the loss, computing and storing every intermediate value. Here's a tiny example. f equals x plus y, times z. Let q be x plus y, so f equals q times z. Take x equals negative two, y equals five, z equals negative four. Forward pass: q is three, and f is negative twelve.

Now the backward pass. We start at the output with d f by d f equals one. Then f equals q times z, so d f by d z is q, which is three, and d f by d q is z, which is negative four. Those are the local gradients of the multiply node. Next, q equals x plus y. The local derivative of q with respect to x is one, and with respect to y is also one. So by the chain rule, d f by d x equals d f by d q times one, which is negative four, and the same for y, also negative four. Notice the pattern. Each node only needs two things: the gradient flowing in from above, which we call the upstream gradient, and its own local derivative. It multiplies them and passes the result down to its inputs. No node needs to know anything about the rest of the graph.

And a couple of patterns are worth memorising. An add gate distributes the upstream gradient unchanged to all its inputs. A multiply gate swaps: each input gets the upstream gradient times the other input. A max gate routes the whole gradient to whichever input was largest and gives zero to the others. What happens if a value is used in two places, so it has two outgoing edges? Then the gradients from both branches add up. That's the multivariable chain rule. Forgetting to sum over branches is one of the most common bugs when people implement backprop by hand. So the cost. The backward pass visits every node once, just like the forward pass, so computing all the gradients costs roughly the same as one or two forward passes. Compare that to numerical differentiation, where you'd need a separate forward pass for every single weight.

Let's put it together on an actual network. Two layers. Input x, hidden layer h equals sigmoid of W one x plus b one, output y hat equals W two h plus b two, and squared error loss, one half times y hat minus y, squared. Forward pass first, and we cache everything: the pre-activation z one, the hidden activations h, and the output y hat. We need those cached values on the way back. This is also why training uses so much more memory than inference, all those activations have to be kept around. Backward pass. The gradient of the loss with respect to y hat is just y hat minus y, the error. Call it delta two. Then the gradient for W two is delta two times h transpose, and the gradient for b two is delta two itself.

Now we push the error back into the hidden layer. The upstream gradient for h is W two transpose times delta two. Then we go through the sigmoid, whose derivative is sigma times one minus sigma, which is h times one minus h, element wise. So delta one equals W two transpose delta two, times h times one minus h. Is that why people say sigmoid networks have vanishing gradients, because that h times one minus h is small? Exactly right. h times one minus h is at most one quarter, at h equals one half. Stack ten sigmoid layers and you've multiplied by at most a quarter ten times, so the gradient at the early layers is tiny. That's a big reason modern networks use ReLU, whose derivative is exactly one wherever it's active.

Finally, the gradient for W one is delta one times x transpose, and for b one it's delta one. Look at the shape of those two results. The gradient for every weight matrix is the error at that layer times the input to that layer. That pattern repeats in every fully connected layer. And how do you know your implementation is right? Gradient checking. Compute a numerical gradient with a centred difference, L of theta plus epsilon minus L of theta minus epsilon, over two epsilon, for a few weights, and compare it with your backprop gradient. The relative error should be around ten to the minus seven. Okay, that's the full loop: forward pass, loss, backward pass, gradient descent update, repeat. For next week, read chapter six of the textbook and do problem set four, which has you implement exactly this two-layer network from scratch. See you Thursday.
